loc: Lesson02_Kubernetes_Foundations_for_Backup_Admins.html · Section 06 · caption under the VolumeSnapshotClass code block
orig: K10 appears inside the annotation key because that is the product's technical namespace in the API; the product name is Veeam Kasten.
prop: k10 appears in lowercase inside the annotation key k10.kasten.io/is-snapshot-class because that key is a verbatim technical string; the product name is Veeam Kasten for Kubernetes.
why: Two problems in one sentence. (1) Naming standard and glossary.md "K10" note: "K10" is permitted only inside verbatim technical strings — but the string in the code block directly above is lowercase (k10.kasten.io/is-snapshot-class), so the caption's uppercase "K10" is not the verbatim string it claims to be and reintroduces the retired product name as prose. (2) "the product's technical namespace in the API" is imprecise — k10.kasten.io is the annotation key's domain prefix, not a Kubernetes namespace, and the module has just spent a section teaching the learner what a namespace is. Same paragraph also carries the only remaining uppercase K10 in the six files, so fixing it clears the naming check course-wide.

loc: Lesson02_Kubernetes_Foundations_for_Backup_Admins.html · section#kasten ("Where Veeam Kasten sits in all of this")
orig: Because it runs as pods among other pods, its security posture is a cluster concern: all Veeam Kasten pods enable a read-only root filesystem security context by default, with writable paths backed by dedicated volume mounts [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1096].
prop: Because it runs as pods among other pods, its security posture is a cluster concern: all Veeam Kasten pods enable a read-only root filesystem security context by default, with writable paths backed by dedicated volume mounts [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1096]. On Red Hat OpenShift specifically, this is also a Security Context Constraint (SCC) question — which SCC the Veeam Kasten pods run under, and whether the cluster's default restricted-v2 SCC is sufficient or a custom SCC is required, is not addressed here [VERIFY: confirm Veeam Kasten's SCC requirements on OpenShift against the installation reference before an architect relies on this section].
why: This course discusses OpenShift extensively (Routes, DeploymentConfig, OAuth proxy, OKD, Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization) and this exact passage is making a hardening/security-posture claim, but Security Context Constraints — the single most common day-one blocker when running third-party Helm charts on OpenShift, and the first thing an OpenShift architect checks before an install — are never mentioned anywhere in the course. An expert reader hits 'its security posture is a cluster concern' and immediately asks 'under which SCC' — leaving that unanswered on an OpenShift-heavy course costs credibility. Flagged as an expertise-based doubt for SME confirmation, not asserted as fact, per the persona's hard rules.

loc: Lesson02_Kubernetes_Foundations_for_Backup_Admins.html · Concept · 06 — Prove it before you design around it ("The pre-flight check is a real test")
orig:
The pre-flight check is a real test

The primer tool runs in a pod in the cluster and creates a sample application with a persistent volume, writes data to it, snapshots the volume, creates a new volume from that snapshot, and validates the data in the new volume [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102].
prop:
The CSI pre-flight check is a real test

Run with a specified StorageClass, the primer tool runs in a pod in the cluster and creates a sample application with a persistent volume, writes data to it, snapshots the volume, creates a new volume from that snapshot, and validates the data in the new volume [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]. Lesson 03 covers both invocations: the basic run, and this one.
why: Scope. The end-to-end round trip on Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102 belongs to the CSI pre-flight check deployed 'with a specified StorageClass' ('… | bash /dev/stdin csi -s ${STORAGE_CLASS}'); the plain primer run validates settings, catalogs StorageClasses and does basic CSI validation (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.7). As written, the foundations lesson tells the learner the default pre-flight already proved the snapshot path — which is exactly the assumption that lets an unverified driver through the readiness gate two lessons later.

orig: Explain why Veeam Kasten treats a namespace as an application, and what that means for how you will scope protection
prop: Explain why Veeam Kasten for Kubernetes treats a namespace as an application, and what that means for how you will scope protection
why: Naming standard: first use of the product name on a page should be the full 'Veeam Kasten for Kubernetes,' with 'Veeam Kasten' after. This lesson's hero blurb never names the product at all, and the objectives list (the first prose mention on the page) drops straight to the short form. Every other lesson opens its blurb with the full name — this is the one page where the pattern breaks. Doesn't affect a demo audience's comprehension, but it's the one naming-standard gap in an otherwise clean course, so it should be closed before this ships as the reference example.

orig: A namespace is a named boundary inside a cluster that holds a set of related objects — workloads, configuration, secrets, storage claims, service definitions. Names are unique within a namespace rather than across the cluster, access control is commonly granted per namespace, and a team is commonly given one to work in. In practice a namespace is how an application is deployed: one namespace, one application, all of its parts inside it.
prop: A namespace is a named boundary inside a cluster that holds a set of related objects — workloads, configuration, secrets, storage claims, service definitions. Names are unique within a namespace rather than across the cluster, access control is commonly granted per namespace, and a team is commonly given one to work in. (On Red Hat OpenShift, which this course also targets, a namespace is wrapped by a Project object that adds default quotas and access policy — the two terms describe the same underlying Kubernetes object [VERIFY: confirm whether Veeam Kasten's own documentation and dashboard use "namespace" or "project" terminology on OpenShift, and note any Project-specific caveat for policy scoping].) In practice a namespace is how an application is deployed: one namespace, one application, all of its parts inside it.
why: The course teaches heavily toward OpenShift (DeploymentConfig, Route, OAuth, OKD) but never once distinguishes "namespace" from OpenShift's Project wrapper — a term an OpenShift-literate reader expects to see addressed the same way the course carefully addresses every other Kubernetes-vs-OpenShift naming nuance. Not a wrong mental model on its own, but a gap in the terminology precision this course otherwise holds itself to.
